cim: Autonomous AI Attack Tools Target Coding Agents, Chatbots and Retail Payment Systems, Infrawatch Finds
cim_eredeti: Autonomous AI Attack Tools Target Coding Agents, Chatbots and Retail Payment Systems, Infrawatch Finds
szoveg_eredeti:
New research from Infrawatch has revealed how threat actors are using autonomous offensive frameworks (AOFs) to launch attacks against organisations, with AI coding agents, customer-facing chatbots, fintech platforms and retail payment systems among the targets.

The findings highlight an emerging dimension of AI security risk: not only are threat actors using AI to facilitate cyberattacks, but they are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure itself, exploiting the autonomy and permissions granted to these systems.

The research, The Autonomy of the Autonomous Intrusions, analysed 128 AI-assisted intrusions and identified 10,848 services running autonomous offensive frameworks across 8,105 hosts globally. The number of servers hosting these frameworks has more than doubled since 6 November 2026.

Researchers also identified more than 130 variants of ARTEX, the most widely used autonomous offensive framework, highlighting the rapid evolution of the AI-powered offensive ecosystem.

In at least 24 of the attacks analysed, threat actors targeted other organisations’ AI infrastructure.

In one instance, an attacker targeted exposed AI coding agents, redirecting them to an attacker-controlled language model and harvesting 77 credentials from compromised machines.

Elsewhere, an autonomous offensive framework testing a fintech company’s production AI service introduced a malicious tool via its Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. Worryingly, the company’s own AI agent discovered, approved and executed the malicious tool without human intervention.

Customer-facing chatbots were also targeted, with attackers extracting an online retailer’s internal chatbot instructions and information about the tools it could access. In another instance, a hotel booking assistant was manipulated into revealing details of its internal functionality.

The research also uncovered attempts to compromise publicly accessible image-generation and local AI inference services, demonstrating the breadth of the emerging AI attack surface.

The use of autonomous offensive frameworks extends beyond traditional network intrusions.

Infrawatch identified a modified version of ARTEX being used in a fraud campaign targeting a multinational retailer’s payment and gift-card infrastructure. Researchers also observed attacks against cryptocurrency exchanges, government databases and e-commerce platforms.

Where researchers could establish the level of human involvement, AI agents were responsible for driving more than 70% of intrusions, either autonomously or under supervision. However, the technology remains imperfect, with hallucinations contributing to unsuccessful attacks.

Familiar vulnerabilities, unprecedented scale

Despite the technological sophistication of autonomous offensive frameworks, the underlying security weaknesses being exploited are largely familiar. Unsecured databases, insufficient authentication and longstanding software vulnerabilities continue to provide opportunities for attackers.

The difference lies in the speed and scale at which these weaknesses can now be identified and exploited, without requiring continuous human involvement.

However, the infrastructure supporting autonomous attacks presents an opportunity for defenders. Infrawatch found that 45% of observed intrusions originated directly from servers hosting autonomous offensive frameworks, making infrastructure intelligence a potentially valuable tool for disrupting malicious activity.

The researchers recommend incorporating infrastructure intelligence into wider cybersecurity strategies, alongside behavioural monitoring, authentication controls and risk-based blocking.

As autonomous offensive frameworks proliferate, organisations face the dual challenge of defending against increasingly automated attacks while ensuring that their own AI deployments do not become new avenues for compromise.
